dedupe_keys.name: united states major space weather risks from coupled physics engineering economic modelling agu advances 2026

description: This case study applies a coupled physics-engineering-economic framework to the United States to estimate what an extreme geomagnetic storm would cost through power grid damage. Edward Oughton and co-authors from George Mason University, the U.S. Geological Survey, NCAR and the University of Cape Town published it in AGU Advances in September 2026, to quantify a hazard whose socio-economic impacts are poorly known. The framework links geophysical drivers to geoelectric fields on the high-voltage grid, transformer thermal vulnerability and macroeconomic consequences, with quantified uncertainty. For a 250-year storm it estimates daily losses of 1.81 billion US dollars from transformer heating alone, affecting about 5.1 million people and 135,000 businesses. Coverage is the contiguous national grid. Format and access: an open-access journal article. Licence: CC BY; free. Caveats: the estimates are lower bounds that leave out voltage collapse, cascading failures and restoration costs, and the inputs are modelled, not observed. It serves hazard exposure and cascading failure assessment of space weather for electricity and the sectors that depend on it. Related catalogue records are the Lloyd's and Cambridge extreme space weather scenario and the Hydro-Québec 1989 blackout.
